INTRODUCTION and ACKNOWLEDGEMENTS

We wish to thank all of you for your enthusiastic
support of our efforts to make this Francis Family reunion
a memorable one. You accepted the project of compiling
a Family Album as an endeavor of value, and your cooperation
made us eager to put together a booklet that you would
be proud of. We hope that we have succeeded.

We thank you also for your time, your attention
to detail, your suggestions, your offers of assistance,
and your Sharing of your skills and talents. We are
especially thankful to those whose UNIQUE CONTRIBUTIONS
made this album and this reunion a reality:

memory, to the values, hard work, and individual attri-

purpose of compiling this album is threefold: (1) to in-
troduce younger.family members to a brief family history,
(2) to enable the family members to get to know one another

family members through positive examples.

A SON’S TRIBUTE

James Henry Francis, and his sister, Ella, were born to Josephine Francis Scott in a single-parent household.
During his early childhood and after his mother’s marriage to Mr. William Scott, Father James and his sister
Ella were sent to live with their grandmother. At this early age, Father was entrusted into the awful
responsibility of becoming the man of the household. This meant tilling a small acreage of land with an ox,
and caring for his ailing grandmother.

Even with an ailing grandmother and a sister to care for, he and his sister attended the public school on a
I somewhat regular basis, and completed a curriculum that would parallel the eighth grade today. They both
/ joined the church and became supportive members. Upon the death of their grandmother, Aunt Ella married
I Mr. James Davis, and Father James chose the young lady of his heart, Miss Pearl Martha Ann Clanton I
I whose family background could be seen closely paralleling that of his own. The difference being, her family fe!
consisted of four sisters: Aunt Hatty, Mary, Josie, and Sally Ann, and one brother, Jimmy as well as her
I mother, Nancy Roberson. Uncle Jimmy and Aunt Sally Ann became very prosperous landowners in their own
: right.

Immediately after marriage, Father and Mother launched into two enterprises that proved rather courageous
and adventurous. They invested their somewhat limited resources in a community grocery store, while at the
same time began rearing a family. Their merchandizing business prospered to the extent that they were able a
to enjoy the distinction of owning a horse and a buggy. A rare status symbol to be enjoyed by such a

newlywed couple in those days. The skill and determination with which this young couple managed their

family and business caught the eyes and won the respect of several community leaders and landowners.

The Reverend Joseph Silver Sr. who held the distinction of being the early organizer of the Holiness Church
in the Eastern USA, guided the young couple into purchasing their first parcel of farmland and dwelling of
sufficient size to accommodate their rapidly increasing family. Approximately 40 acres were purchased in
the initial transaction, and was followed by the purchase of approximately 150 additional acres later. By the
year 1920, this couple had achieved a status that became the envy of their neighbors and friends. Home
ownership, land ownership, and a healthy family of eight children as of that date, constituted a prosperous
farming business.

One of the rewarding aspects of this couple’s blessing of prosperity could be seen in their simple but unique
philosophy. They believed that sacrifice and hard work were cornerstones to success when these elements
undergird a well defined purpose and determination to achieve. This philosophy could also be seen in the
emphasis our parents placed on education, thrift, work ethics, religion, respect for oneself, and the respect
for others. They considered the family as a unique social unit that is endowed with the responsibility of
Sustaining itself, and structured in such a way as to provide the leadership, discipline, and citizenship
directions throughout one’s entire social life.

Fr? *

As the years rolled by, the family and the farming enterprise increased and prospered. Another member was
added to the family practically every year. As the family continued to increase, our parents sought to fulfill
their obligation of passing onto the their children certain intrinsic values they felt would certainly be needed
in order to compete successfully in an increasingly complex society. They felt that education for survival
begins in the home. With this concept, a rather unique "Family-shared Work Assignment Program" was
instituted. Our parents felt that each member of the family should, within the limits of his or her talent and
capability, contribute to the general welfare of the whole family. Therefore, each family member was
assigned a specific area of family living, and was held accountable for accomplishment of the family’s

performance goals. I

Two boys were held responsible for feeding and caring for the teams of mules; two were caretakers of the
hogs; one was to care for the chickens; one was held responsible for milking the cows and processing the I
milk and butter; two boys were assigned to the vegetable garden; one of the girls did the laundry; one girl I
served as assistant cook and the others were assigned minor jobs in the cooperative-living plan. Everybody, I
however, was required to make-up their own beds in the morning, go to Sunday school and church on I
Sundays, be home before sundown, and if one were of the acceptable courting age, he had to be at home

before 10:00 p.m.

The boys were allowed to try their hand at enterprising. One sold the Grit Newspaper; one sold Cloverine
Healing Salves; one sold garden seeds; one handled dairy products; one ran a small country store; one
raised squabs and poultry, and another did some roadside bartering of roasted peanuts and peanut candy
along the roadside with laborers who would travel to and from their jobs at the small country town of Delmar,
North Carolina, located by the railroad adjacent to our farm. No one got rich in these small ventures, but
much was learned and ambitions stimulated as a result of the tolerance and character-development skills of

these parents.

: ~

In the Fall of 1923. the family’s loyalty and cooperation were rewarded with a brand new 1923 Model T Ford
automobile. Even though it was a standard size car of that day, it had to have been built of special steel,
since the entire family of 13 children would be packed into the car on Sunday afternoons with Mama in the
front seat holding baby Claude, Calvin in the middle peeping over the dash board, and Papa in the driver's
seat. This mode of travel meant good-bye to traveling to church on Sunday and grocery shopping in town
in a wagon drawn by a team of mules. With this euphoria of progress, tragedy had to come. It did in the
form of the sudden death of our youngest brother of five months, Jeremiah Douglas, a victim of an untimely
accident. This Deing the first death within the family, the grief that it brought served to remind the family that
we also are merely children of destiny.

The progress of these two parents became even more obvious over the next three years when in 1926, a
new Model T Ford truck was added in order to give greater mobility to the farming operation. With the
purchase of an additional tract of farm land in 1927, the family finally entered the industrial farming era. This
necessitated the purchase of the first farm tractor and implements.

This brought the family to another pressing need, the accommodation for the growth and development of 13
children. Within the midst of a great depression in 1928, our parents ventured out to build a new home; a
modern 9-room, 2 story structure with the convenience very much up-to-date in those days. With the help
of the older brothers and three carpenters and a mason, our family home was completed during the Fall of
1928. Even though our home was built before Rural Electrification became available, our home was equipped
with modern gas lights, a bathroom and basement. This self-help achievement was rewarded by the
purchase of a Ford roadsier car for the boys, and later a new Chevrolet Sedan car for the family.

The next major concern of our parents was the education of their children. There being no available high
school for students of our race within the immediate vicinity, the older sons were sent off to high school at
Weldon and later to Henderson Institute.

When the Eastman High School at Ringwood, N.C. extended its patronage area to include our community,
Our parents were financially instrumental in securing the first school bus which made it possible for the
children to secure a high school education. As a result, three of the children went on to college. The
religious education was not overlooked. The family rule was "religious commitment must precede all other
commitments whether they be economic, political, or social". The commitment to Christ, joining the church,
and attending Sunday School were top priorities. The boys weren't allowed to use the car, and the girls
weren't allowed to entertain their boyfriends until after they had attended church services and Sunday School.
Even though the children were taught the importance of discipline and thrift, they were also reminded that
the church and other worthy institutions serving those who aren’t so fortunate should undergird all our efforts
toward financial achievement.

As the years passed, and while some of the children grew into adulthood and some married, World War II
came along. six of the men of the family had to answer the draft, five of whom served overseas, two served
in the combat zone in the Army. Grady and Wilbert served in the Navy, while Claude, Calvin, and Jesse
served in the Army. Other brothers served in critical defense industries on the homefront. It had to have

been Mama’s prayers and the mercy of God that all of the sons returned from the war without any major
injuries.

8

During the post-war years, our parents continued to prosper. The farming business of approximately 200
acres had become completely mechanized with the latest technology, equipment, and farming methods, But,
by the time Mother and Dad had begun to feel the wear and tear of the years, and the children began to
appreciate the wisdom of their counsel and cherished value of their presence, Dad found it necessary to retire
from his role as manager. He finally turned the farming operation over to the youngest son, Claude, who
had been the assistant operator since his return form the service in 1946.

Mother and Dad continued to serve their church and community well. Dad continued to serve as trustee
chairman, and Mother as the "Mother of the church”. After 87 years of faithful service to his family,
community, church and country, Dad passed away on April 16, 1973. Five years later, at the age of 88 years,
our dear Mother passed on Christmas Day, December, 1978.

To say the least, we children are so grateful and thankful to our Creator for the exceedingly rich heritage of
- having been*born, taught, cared for, and motivated by such wise and caring parents, who, in spite of the

limited economic, social, and educational opportunities of their youth, rose above those handicaps and made

a significant and lasting contribution to their children, the community, their church, and( their prosperity>* )
